newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Tutsi rebels agree to Zaire refugee corridor.
newsitem.headline: Tutsi rebels agree to Zaire refugee corridor.

text.p: Tutsi rebels controlling a swathe of eastern Zaire have agreed to open up a humanitarian corridor to enable relief workers to reach Hutu refugees trapped and scattered by fighting in the area.

Relief groups in Rwanda, which is accused by Kinshasa of fomenting the revolt, said the Tutsi-led government there had agreed to let food and medicine across the border into eastern Zaire, where death and disease threaten over a million Hutus.

But as night fell on Sunday, two mortar rounds hit the rebel-held city of Goma -- a reminder that well-armed Rwandan Hutu militias who have been fighting the rebels alongside Zairean troops have not given up the battle for the town.

"We have reached an agreement with them (rebels) and we'll be sending in assessment teams first thing tomorrow," Omar Backhet, resident representative of the U.N. Development Programme (UNDP) in Rwanda, told Reuters in the capital Kigali.
"The teams will be made up of non-governmental agencies and within a day or two U.N. agencies should be able to go in as well," he said late on Sunday.
In Paris, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali made a new appeal for immediate world intervention to help the refugees, saying thousands were dying with every passing hour.
"Two years ago the international community was confronted by a genocide of the Tutsis by arms. Today we are confronted by a genocide of the Hutus by famine," he said on his way to Rome.
Over a million Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after Hutu hardliners massacred up to a million minority Tutsis and their sympathisers.

They fled once again when ethnic Tutsis, many of whom have lived in Zaire for generations, launched a revolt near the border with Burundi just over three weeks ago. The rebels now control most towns in the eastern refugee provinces.
Hundreds of thousands of Hutus from Burundi and displaced Zaireans have also fled the fighting. The whereabouts of many in the sprawling and chaotic Central African nation are unknown.
But refugees say many armed Hutu hardliners have gathered in Mugunga refugee camp -- the world's biggest -- near Goma.
The roots of the crisis are in Hutu-Tutsi hatred that has blighted life in Rwanda and Burundi for generations.
Zaire accuses Rwanda of invading its territory. Rwanda accuses Zaire of tacitly supporting the Hutu hardliners who lived among the refugees and launched cross-border raids.
But the estranged Central African neighbours have both backed the return to Rwanda of the Hutu refugees.

EU humanitarian commissioner Emma Bonino held talks with Zaire's government on Sunday and said that any repatriation of refugees had to be voluntary. "I am opposed to any forced repatriation," she told reporters in Kinshasa.

But diplomats say she too favours a return of the refugees. "I think our explanation has also reassured the (Zairean) authorities that it is not our intention to restore permanent camps. That's to say to return to square one," Bonino said.

Earlier, U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien failed to win Zairean support for safe havens inside Zaire. "It's extremely frustrating for me to see more obstacles presenting themselves than possible solutions," he said in Kinshasa.
He later arrived in Rwanda after talks in Uganda.
Bonino and her EU team head for Rwanda on Monday. One diplomat in Kigali said she favoured a corridor "so aid can reach the refugees and so that they also return home".
